_comment: How the repository scan agent evolved: the self-improvement loop run behind results/synthetic.md, on all the pairs it
ran on: the public synthetic benchmark and two benchmarks we can't publish, as aggregate counts only. Per version of
the agent: pairs right of the 72 training pairs the loop measured it on, and of the 47 held-out validation pairs;
fixed twins flagged on each. A pair is right when the agent reports the planted lines in the vulnerable repository
and nothing at the same lines of its fixed twin. The loop ran in two stages. In stage 1 a version was kept only with
at least 3 more validation pairs right than the best so far; none was, so all three were built on the start. Stage 2
started from stage 1's best on the training pairs and kept a version when it got more training pairs right. Version 6
was not eligible (its steps failed on too many repositories), so it was not scanned on the validation pairs. The
version presented is the one with the most validation pairs right; its test result is on 46 test pairs nothing in
the loop had seen. Per version, what the optimizer changed: our own one-line summary, the size of the change against
the version it was built on, and a few of the lines it added (from its prompt, its tools, its pipeline). The
optimizer's own notes are not used: they cite repositories of the benchmarks we can't publish.

stages.label: Stage 1: kept only with 3 more validation pairs right
Stage 2: kept with more training pairs right

versions.label: Start
versions.summary: The starting point, written by hand and deliberately weak: a short prompt, and tools to read files and run Python.

Knows what to look for: a long prompt on where untrusted input enters a Haystack component and what safe code looks like, a search tool, higher limits, and a last check that withdraws findings on code a safeguard protects.
highlights: How Haystack components receive untrusted input:
- eval(x) on untrusted input = VULNERABLE. ast.literal_eval(x) = SAFE (do not report).

versions.summary: Adds a first pass that searches the repository for dangerous calls and reports them itself. It flags far more lines, and gets fewer pairs right.
highlights: DESCRIPTION = "Hunter step: search the repository for dangerous sink patterns and report real vulnerabilities as candidates, using the model only to triage ambiguous cases."

versions.summary: A narrower first pass: a fixed list of dangerous calls, each one checked by the model before it is reported.
highlights: (r"\beval\s*\(", "CWE-94", "Code injection via eval() on untrusted input", "eval("),

versions.summary: Names more kinds of defect in the prompt, such as a request without a timeout or a secret in a URL. It also adds a pre-scan step, but nothing passes its notes to the agent.
highlights: Additional classes to look for (these are common in this benchmark):
- Secret appended to a URL as a query parameter = VULNERABLE (CWE-598). Authorization header = SAFE.

versions.summary: Names more defects with the safeguard that fixes each, such as missing escaping or a path that leaves its folder, and tells the agent not to chase missing timeouts.
highlights: - Missing HTML escaping: document text interpolated raw into HTML = VULNERABLE (CWE-79). escape_html() before interpolation = SAFE.

versions.summary: Adds a step that moves each finding to the exact vulnerable line. Its steps failed on too many repositories, so it was not eligible and not scanned on the validation pairs.
highlights: DESCRIPTION = "Refine each finding: move it to the exact vulnerable statement by reading the surrounding code and asking the model to pinpoint the vulnerable line. Only moves a finding when confident; otherwise keeps the original location."

versions.summary: Connects the pre-scan step, so its notes reach the agent, and names more defects in the prompt. It does slightly worse on both sets.

note: The counts include two benchmarks we can't publish.
